items.summary_raw: OSINTdefender The U.S. military has sent additional Patriot air defense missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, according to two U.S. officials and a regional source who spoke to Axios. One battery went to a Saudi oil facility, another to a Qatari gas facility, officials say the move is meant to reassure both allies their energy infrastructure will be protected if President Trump resumes major strikes on Iran. Officials from U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) declined to comment.  President Donald J. Trump said Thursday he's weighing renewed bombing in the coming weeks: "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer." Officials say Saudi and Qatari leaders lobbied Trump in August against striking Iranian energy infrastructure, warning of retaliation against their own facilities, and that this was a key reason he pulled back toward economic pressure instead at the time. The U.S. is expected to need Saudi airspace access for any renewed operations. items.title: Eastern Spain braces for torrential rain and flooding
items.summary_raw:
Up to 300mm of rain could fall in places, while extreme downpours bring landslides and deaths in Nepal

Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.

Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.

Russia will also reportedly target the electrical switchyards at the Rivne, Khmelnytskyi, and South-Ukraine Nuclear Power Plants.   In Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa, Russia reportedly plans to cut electricity and heating by 90%, while causing significant disruption to their water sewerage system. The strike campaign will reportedly take place in three stages, starting with targeting electrical substation near the western borders of Ukraine used to transfer European-supplies electricity, before moving to hydro-electric power plants, and then targeting nuclear power plants at the end.   In my opinion, 1,000 missiles, drones, and glide-bombs is a massive undercount. According to available information, Russia has over 12,000 Geran-2 drones in reserve, a portion of which they will likely use during the winter for strikes on energy targets. The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, a report has found, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C.

Surface air temperatures in western Europe from June to August were 2.5C above the recent decadal average, according to an update from the EU’s Copernicus climate monitoring service on Friday, while milder but still deadly heat across the rest of the continent made the summer Europe’s third hottest on record.

The Cyprus-flagged cargo ship Västerbotten departed Sweden on September 29 and was due to arrive in Estonia on October 1. After entering Russian territorial waters, it was stopped and ordered to anchor in the Gulf of Finland. Russian border guards inspected the vessel for several hours before allowing it to continue toward Estonia.  The vessel’s eventual release kept the incident from developing into a larger confrontation, but the detention adds a new maritime dimension to tensions in the Baltic. If such actions become more frequent, commercial shipping could increasingly find itself caught in the broader sanctions confrontation between Russia and European states. items.title: New Tensions with Ankara over Greece-Cyprus Electricity Cable
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS - The Greece-Cyprus electricity interconnection project is entering a new phase of tension, with Ankara insisting that it will not allow the cable to be laid without prior Turkish authorization, while Athens categorically rejects the demand, citing international law and the Law of the Sea. Turkey’s Defense Ministry, in a new statement, reiterated that it will not permit cable-laying work without Turkey’s approval, arguing that part of the planned survey activity will take place in an area that Ankara considers to be part of the Turkish continental shelf. The Greek government, for its part, insists that no Turkish authorization is required. Government spokesperson Pavlos Marinakis has said that “there is no issue of authorization” and that the project will proceed on the basis of international law. “We will not rewrite international law because one country does not like it,” he said.

items.title: 66th Anniversary of the Republic of Cyprus’ Independence Honored with Splendor
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – The 66th anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic of Cyprus was celebrated with great splendor, including a large military parade in Nicosia. Attention centered on the National Guard’s new weapons systems, the flyovers by Greek F-16 fighter aircraft, and the presence of military contingents from five countries. The presence of modern missile, anti-aircraft, and unmanned systems reflected the modernization of the National Guard’s arsenal and the significant upgrading of the Cypriot military’s operational capabilities in recent years. A special moment that stirred deep emotion was the appearance in the skies over Nicosia of Greek F-16 Vipers, which took off from the ‘Andreas Papandreou’ air base in Paphos. The F-16 Vipers, which flew at low altitude over Iosif Hadjiiosif Avenue, where the parade took place, are the most modern upgraded version of the F-16s operated by the Hellenic Air Force. They are equipped with advanced AESA radar, a new mission computer, and upgraded communications systems.

items.title: ‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years
items.summary_raw:
Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution

Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years, research has found, in a dramatic reshaping of the Alpine country whose big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say.

Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%.

items.title: UK banks are Europe’s biggest coal financiers, report finds
items.summary_raw:
Study says UK-based banks provided $8.3bn in coal financing in four years, with Barclays and HSBC leading rise

UK banks are Europe’s biggest financial backers of the global coal industry, providing billions of pounds in funding for the climate-wrecking fossil fuel in the past four years, according to a report.

The study found UK-based banks had provided $8.3bn (£6.2bn) in coal financing since Cop26 in Glasgow in 2021, when global leaders pledged to “phase down” coal use. This compared with $4.9bn from German banks and $3.4bn from French banks over the same period.

items.title: California rushes to prepare for massive ‘Kelvin’ wave and predicted sea level rise
items.summary_raw:
Wave nearing southern California expected to reach San Francisco Bay Area by October as it crawls toward Alaska

Communities across California are rushing to prepare for the imminent arrival of the so-called “Kelvin wave”, a massive underwater band of warm water threatening to inundate swaths of the vast North American shoreline.

The wave is nearing southern California and expected to reach the San Francisco Bay Area by early October, as it crawls toward Alaska. Waters could rise by a foot along the California coast, according to scientists, who have warned that this could dramatically double the 8-12in rise in sea levels already caused by climate change over the last century.

items.title: Libya's secret executions: Why now?
items.summary_raw:
Libya's secret executions: Why now?

At least 30 men have been executed in eastern Libya after being sentenced to death in secret military trials by the Libyan Armed Forces, under commander Khalifa Haftar, for the first time since 2010.

Human Rights Watch's Ahmed Benchemsi tells Mathilda Mallinson on MEE Live that the executions have been able to go ahead now due to lack of accountability against actors in the region and international actors with interests in Libyan factions.

Qatar proposed a deal linking Iran’s demand to lift the U.S. naval blockade with U.S. demands for nuclear concessions. But Iran said it would only consider nuclear steps if Washington returned to the June memorandum of understanding.  U.S. officials initially described the talks as positive and said Trump was open to sanctions relief and releasing frozen funds for nuclear concessions. Hours later, Trump said he had offered Iran nothing.  A source told Axios the talks were “stuck,” while Trump said Tuesday that Iran “will give up” and “will not have a nuclear weapon.”  Source: Axios

items.title: OSINTdefender The Department of War has confirmed the Navy's F/A-XX contract award to Boeing, officially announcing what Breaking Defense reported today, citing sources, just hours…
items.summary_raw: OSINTdefender The Department of War has confirmed the Navy's F/A-XX contract award to Boeing, officially announcing what Breaking Defense reported today, citing sources, just hours earlier. The contract is valued at more than $20 billion for full-scale development, covering multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems, and weapons integration testing.  Part of the Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD) program, F/A-XX will augment and eventually replace the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler starting in the 2030s, operating alongside the carrier variant F-35C. The Navy says it will also be interoperable with Collaborative Combat Aircraft, increasing the capability of every CCA it teams with.  "The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength," said Michael Duffey, Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment, adding the program will help "deter aggression, project undisputed power, and secure absolute air superiority." Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao called it "a generational leap in air superiority."  The award makes Boeing the sole U.S. producer of sixth-generation fighters, having already won the Air Force's F-47

items.title: Rubio says Iran would 'blackmail the world' if it had a nuclear weapon
items.summary_raw:
Rubio says Iran would 'blackmail the world' if it had a nuclear weapon

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that if Iran had a nuclear weapon, it would use it to "blackmail the world and to kill people".

"It would control the straits, charge a toll, and decide who got energy and who did not," Rubio said during an interview with Fox News, and added that this could present an "unacceptable risk".

He also accused Tehran of using money received through sanctions relief or economic selling to build weapons and "export the revolution" rather than to "improve the lives of the Iranian people".

"They use the money to fund Hezbollah, they use the money to fund Hamas, they use the money to fund Shia militias in Iraq… they use the money to sponsor terrorism and assassination plots," Rubio said. <

items.title: The Cyprus Issue at the Center of the Cyprus Federation Dinner
items.summary_raw:
NEW YORK. Efforts to restart talks on the Cyprus issue, as well as the longstanding role of the Greek-American community in promoting Cyprus’ positions in Washington, were at the center of the annual dinner hosted by the Federation of Cypriot American Organizations on Friday evening, September 25, at Terrace on the Park. The event, held, as every year, in the presence of the government delegation of the Republic of Cyprus attending the U.N. General Assembly and headed by President Nikos Christodoulides, honored three members of the Cypriot-American community for their contributions. The Lifetime Achievement Award was presented to John Josephakis, NVIDIA’s Global Vice President of Sales and Business Development for High Performance Computing and Supercomputing. The Community Service Award was presented to Stavros Kamilaris, president of the Lampousa Cypriot American Association, and Despina Axiotakis, former executive director of the Cyprus-U.S. Chamber of Commerce, for her many years of service to the community.

items.title: Ex-Haniyeh Bodyguard Held in London
items.summary_raw:
A former bodyguard to Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh was granted asylum in Britain, later received permanent residency and became a British citizen, The Sunday Times reports.

Years later, he was arrested in London over a Hamas linked plot to attack Jewish and Israeli targets across Europe.

German prosecutors say he helped move weapons and recorded a masked claim of responsibility video.

He now remains in UK custody.

items.title: U.S. Troops, Ecuadorian Cops Take Down Cartel Jalisco Network in South America
items.summary_raw:

items.title: Israeli forces kill Palestinian in Gaza, arrest four farmers in West Bank
items.summary_raw:
Israeli forces kill Palestinian in Gaza, arrest four farmers in West Bank

Israeli forces shot and killed a Palestinian man in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, Wafa news agency reported, citing sources at Gaza City’s al-Shifa Hospital.

Wafa also reported that several Palestinians, including a child, were wounded in an Israeli drone attack on the outskirts of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, while eastern parts of the city came under Israeli artillery fire.

Israeli forces arrested four Palestinian farmers while they were harvesting olives on their land east of Tulkarem in the occupied West Bank, according to Wafa.

The farmers were working near the Israeli settlement of Einav when they were detained.

Wafa said more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza by Israeli forces
